Chapter 5B

Size, money flows and the six structural shifts

How big the industry is, where the new money is going, the six forces reshaping it, what allocators demand, five views of the next three to five years, and the four flows between a bank and a hedge fund.

5.10 How big is it, and where is the money going?

$5.6tn
Global hedge fund capital, end June 2026, a record [S150c]
$428bn
Goldman's multi-manager universe, 57 platforms, end 2025 [S158] (snippet)
$39 of $44.5bn
Q1 2026 net inflows that went to firms over $5bn [S150b]
12.5%
Average hedge fund return in 2025, best since 2009 [S150a]

The industry passed $5 trillion at the end of 2025 and reached a record $5.6 trillion by mid-2026 after "the largest increase in history" in a single quarter [S150a][S150c] Confirmed. Nearly all of the new money goes to the biggest managers [S150b]. Multi-manager platforms are a minority of assets by AUM, roughly 8% in Goldman's universe, but because they run four to six times gross leverage their market footprint is far larger than that share Inferred. The IMF says the top ten hedge funds "now account for more than one-third of the gross notional exposure across all hedge funds, up from just 20 percent a decade ago" [S152] Confirmed.

Source uncertain

Inflow numbers differ wildly by provider. HFR reports $115.8bn of net inflows in 2025; With Intelligence reports about $59bn across six quarters to mid-2026 [S150a][S162]. Different universes and methods. Say "depending on the data provider" if you quote either.

5.11 The six structural shifts

1. Capital concentrating in large platforms

Allocators want scale, infrastructure and steady returns. More than one in five allocation intentions in the first half of 2026 targeted multi-strategy funds; Millennium received "Multiple $5+ billion allocations" and a "$10 billion WorldQuant partnership" [S162] Reported. Consequence for you: more PMs means more meeting demand.

2. The talent war

Point72 hired one PM with a package of "tens of millions" over five years; Millennium hired a PM who generated $250m in 2024 on a "multimillion-dollar guaranteed deal"; another PM hired by Millennium from Citadel was "intercepted by Balyasny before sit-out period ended" and "Never worked a day at Millennium" [S160a] Reported. Steve Cohen: "no different than baseball." By 2026 "Top managers are now commanding guaranteed nine-figure payouts and multi-year contracts" [S160b]. The pipeline response is structured internships: Citadel's COO said "You can't only hire from the outside. You need to develop even more talent internally now" [S168]. That is part of why your programme exists.

3. Fees: headline down, all-in up

Average fees keep drifting down, but 83% of multi-managers now use pass-through, up from 63% in 2022 [S158]. Balyasny's main fund made 15.2% gross and 2.8% net in 2023 after $768m of pass-through costs, 87% of it pay; Citadel's three largest funds charged $12.5bn of pass-through over 2022 to September 2024 [S156] Reported. BNP Paribas data suggests investors kept roughly 40 to 60 cents of every gross dollar at multi-strategy funds, depending on year and method [S157]. The pushback is organised: Texas Teachers' open letter demanding cash hurdles grew to 60-plus asset owners, and about three-quarters of its managers agreed [S167a][S157] Confirmed.

4. Capacity limits and capital returns

Citadel returned about $5bn of 2025 profits in early 2026, shrinking to around $67bn, "constraining capital to better match" the opportunity set [S165] Confirmed. Millennium has done the opposite: raised $10bn of deployable capital in 2024 and a $5bn private-markets fund in 2025, its first new fund in over 30 years [S173a][S173b]. Business Insider framed its problem as "$86.3 billion and not nearly enough people to invest it" [S168] Reported.

5. Systematic and quant growth

Barclays finds allocators prefer equity market neutral, quant multi-strategy and macro; 55% of investors have put AI into their investment process; discretionary managers are "embedding quantitative tools to expand coverage capacity without proportional headcount" [S171] Reported. Systematic funds gained 4% in March 2025 while stock-pickers lost 2.4% [S163].

6. Leverage, crowding and the regulators

Hedge funds' gross exposure to rates derivatives and government bonds "more than doubled, rising to over $18 trillion in 2025 from less than $9 trillion in 2020" [S152]. The Bank of England reports hedge fund borrowing in the gilt repo market of "close to £100 billion" with "a small number of hedge funds" accounting for over 90%, often "at zero or near-zero collateral haircuts" [S154a], and its July 2026 report says "There has been a substantial rise in hedge fund leverage in equity markets, creating risks, including via the prime brokers" and that hedge fund deleveraging amplified gilt moves in the February to March 2026 shock [S154b] Confirmed. The Financial Stability Board's toolkit is minimum haircuts, central clearing and concentration add-ons, while conceding that "Entity-level leverage measures are less common for entities with multiple, complex strategies, such as hedge funds" [S153].

Key term: de-grossing

Cutting longs and shorts at once because risk limits bite. When many pods hold the same names and all cut together, prices gap. Episodes: March 2020, January 2021, March to April 2025 (Citadel -0.8% and Millennium -2% in Q1 2025 [S163]), and February to March 2026. The IMF says financial stress "has become more correlated with hedge fund losses since 2020" [S152].

@@f49@@
Figure 49. Six forces and their direction for Millennium's model and for in-house corporate access. Basis: [S150b][S158][S157][S161][S152][S154b][S181][S199][S212][S254]. Arrow lengths are the author's judgement, not data, 4 Sep 2026.

5.12 Who gives hedge funds money, and what they demand

Who. Pension funds, insurers, sovereign wealth funds, endowments, funds of funds, family offices and private banks [S151][S171]. In 2026 family offices and private banks are "leading renewed enthusiasm"; 64% of allocators surveyed by BNP Paribas plan to increase hedge fund exposure [S171][S172] Reported. Named 2026 allocations include CalSTRS, Virginia Retirement System, North Carolina (to Balyasny) and Ohio teachers [S162].

What they want. Net returns above cash ("Everyone brings up the fees, but all I care about are net returns" [S160a]); low correlation to equities (multi-strategy beta about 0.24 and volatility about four times lower than world equities [S172]); cash hurdles; a floor on the share of gross return they keep; and increasingly separately managed accounts for transparency [S171].

How terms are set. Through share classes and side letters: ExodusPoint added a Treasury-linked performance fee with a longer lock-up [S166]; Man Group applied pass-through only to new capital [S178b]; Millennium's new fund has a two-year commitment, 20% performance fee and pass-through costs [S173a]. Consultants such as Meketa, NEPC and Cambridge Associates sit on the allocator's side [S167a].

A. Big platforms keep winningRecord $5.6tn with inflows to $5bn+ firms [S150c]; multi-manager AUM +16% in 2025 [S158]; Millennium +15% (2024), +10.5% (2025), +8.2% to August 2026 [S174][S169][S170]Returns trail the S&P 500 in a bull year; capacityYes. Strongest documentary base.
B. The model has peakedMulti-strategy net outflows over $30bn in the year to June 2024 [S159]; Balyasny 15.2% gross to 2.8% net [S156]; Eisler wound down after -14.3% with losses "stemmed from pass-through expenses" [S161]; closures of Atlantic Wolf, Taproot, Eminence, AB Arya in 2026 [S162]The top four or five keep compounding and taking inflowsYes, if you say "peaked for mid-tier platforms".

Your opinion goes here

The author's synthesis: A at the top, B in the middle, C as the constraint that decides how far A can go, and E as Millennium's specific answer to capacity. The cleanest one-line contrast for an interview: Citadel returned $5bn while Millennium raised $5bn for illiquids. Two responses to the same capacity problem. Decide which you think is right and why.

5.14 Sell side and buy side: the four flows between a bank and a hedge fund

The buy side "purchase[s] securities" (investment managers, pension funds, hedge funds). The sell side "issue[s], sell[s], or trade[s] securities" (investment banks, brokers) and "earn[s] their way through fees and commissions" [S176a]. A bank does four things for a fund like Millennium:

  1. Prime brokerage. Lends cash and securities, holds custody, clears trades. Earns financing spreads and stock-loan fees. The most important flow, because it is the source of leverage [S176c].
  2. Execution. Trades the fund's orders. Paid by commission or spread.
  3. Research. Analysts' reports and models. Since MiFID II in 2018 paid separately from execution; since the UK's PS24/9 in 2024 there is a "joint payments" option again under conditions [S179a]. chapter 6A.
  4. Corporate access. Meetings with company management. Under UK rules not research and not payable from client commission, so the fund pays from its own resources or values it in the broker vote. This is your seat.

An analyst on the sell side covers a sector and publishes for many clients, ranked by broker votes. An analyst on the buy side works for one pod, builds private models, and is paid on the pod's profit [S175][S176a].

If asked "why a hedge fund and not a bank?"

Structure: on the sell side, corporate access is a product sold to many clients. On the buy side it is procured, allocated and measured for internal clients who are paid on results. You are the client side of every broker relationship. At a multi-manager the allocation problem is hardest, because hundreds of independent teams compete for the same slot. Then add your own reason. Never disparage banks: at least one of your interviewers appears to have started on a bank's corporate access desk (chapter 10A).

@@c5C@@
Chapter 5C

What is happening to hedge funds right now

Nine forces, as of 4 September 2026, drawn from industry reports (HFR, Barclays, BNP Paribas, With Intelligence, Goldman Sachs as reported), regulator publications (Bank of England, Federal Reserve, IMF, FSB) and the trade press. The short answer to "is it fundraising, trust, or war?" is: fundraising is strong but narrow; trust is contested on fees; war and shocks tested the model twice this year and it mostly held.

5.15 The dashboard

@@f50@@
Figure 50. The 2026 dashboard. Colours are the author's judgement; every figure is sourced as marked and detailed in 5.16 to 5.24. As of 4 September 2026.

5.16 Money: fundraising is strong, and narrow

If you only remember one thing: hedge funds are not short of money in 2026. HFR's industry capital series reads $5.15tn at the end of 2025, $5.22tn at the end of March 2026 and a record $5.6tn at the end of June, after a quarterly rise of about $409bn, "the largest increase in history", and "15 consecutive quarters" of growth [S150a][S150b][S150c] Confirmed. HFR's president: "The current environment is unequivocally the strongest for hedge fund capital growth since industry inception" [S150c]. Reuters reports that "every major hedge fund strategy brought in fresh capital during the first half, a first in five years" [S221]. Barclays' survey of 340-plus investors found net interest at its highest since 2018, and 43% expecting to be net allocators in the second half [S171][S139b] Reported.

@@f51@@
Figure 51. Industry capital and where new money goes. HFR [S150a][S150b][S150c]; With Intelligence for the alternative count [S162].

Who is giving. Family offices and private banks are "leading renewed enthusiasm" [S171]; named 2026 allocations include CalSTRS narrowing a $4bn underweight, Virginia's retirement system deploying $1.3bn, and North Carolina putting $500m with Balyasny [S162]. More than one in five allocation intentions in the first half targeted multi-strategy funds [S162]. What they want. Low correlation to equities, net returns above cash, and increasingly separately managed accounts for transparency: about a quarter of investors now use them [S171][S172].

Source uncertain

Inflow figures vary by an order of magnitude between providers because they count different fund universes. The direction (positive, concentrated in the largest firms) is consistent across HFR, With Intelligence and Barclays. The exact totals are not.

5.17 Trust: the fee fight

"Trust" in 2026 is mostly about money, not scandal. The issue is how much of what a fund earns reaches the investor. Multi-manager platforms pass their costs through, and those costs are large: Balyasny's main fund made 15.2% gross in 2023 and 2.8% net, after $768m of pass-through of which 87% was pay; ExodusPoint made 11% gross with 8.4% of pass-through; Citadel's three largest funds charged $12.5bn of pass-through between 2022 and September 2024, $11bn of it compensation [S156] Reported (Bloomberg analysis of SEC filings). BNP Paribas data, as reported, suggests investors kept about 41 cents of each gross dollar at multi-strategy funds in 2023, down from 54 cents in 2021, though a second report quotes the same series differently, so use a range [S157].

@@f52@@
Figure 52. What investors keep. BNP Paribas via Hedgeweek [S157]; Bloomberg via Hedgeweek [S156]; Texas Teachers coalition [S167a]; LCH Investments [S134]. All press estimates; no fund publishes these figures.

The defence is simple and, so far, winning: net returns after everything have been good. HFR's average fund made 12.5% in 2025, the best year since 2009 [S150a]; multi-strategy funds run a beta to equities of about 0.24 [S172]; and capacity at the best firms is rationed, so investors queue. Texas Tech's Clinton Huff: "Everyone brings up the fees, but all I care about are net returns" [S160a]. The counter-evidence is the mid-tier: at Eisler, "the bulk of the losses stemmed from pass-through expenses, including staff compensation and operational costs charged directly to investors, rather than trading performance" [S161] Reported. Transparency is the other trust lever: about 25% of investors now use separately managed accounts, which let them see positions, and half of funds offer them [S171].

Your opinion goes here

Is pass-through fair? One view: fair while net returns beat what the investor could get elsewhere for the same volatility, and only then. The other: investors bear netting risk and fund the talent war, so hurdles are the minimum. Pick one and say what would change your mind.

5.18 Talent: the industry's biggest cost

Because platforms pay each team on its own profit and pass the bill to investors, the price of portfolio managers has become the central economic fact of the model. Reported examples: Point72 hired one PM with a package of "tens of millions" over five years after competition from Citadel, Millennium and Balyasny; Millennium hired a PM who had generated $250m in 2024 on a "multimillion-dollar guaranteed deal"; another, hired by Millennium from Citadel, was "intercepted by Balyasny before sit-out period ended" and "Never worked a day at Millennium" [S160a] Reported (WSJ via Hedgeweek). Steve Cohen: "We're seeing a lot of firms competing for great talent, no different than baseball" [S160a]. By 2026 "Top managers are now commanding guaranteed nine-figure payouts and multi-year contracts" [S160b], and the fights have gone to court: Schonfeld sued a PM who reversed a move for $11m; Millennium is seeking about $2.5m from a Hong Kong PM who abandoned an offer [S232][S233].

The response is to grow talent rather than buy it. Citadel's COO: "You can't only hire from the outside. You need to develop even more talent internally now" [S168]. Millennium took 190 interns in 2025 from about 50,000 applications and launched an investing internship for 2027 [S271][S168]. That is why structured internship programmes, including the one you applied to, exist.

5.19 Leverage: why central banks are watching

@@f53@@
Figure 53. Leverage numbers. IMF [S152]; Federal Reserve [S155a]; Bank of England [S154a][S154b][S154c][S240][S241]; FSB [S153]. All primary regulator documents.
Key term: repo and haircut

A repo (repurchase agreement) is selling a bond and agreeing to buy it back later at a slightly higher price: economically a secured loan with the bond as collateral. The haircut is the safety cushion the lender demands. The BoE and FSB both note hedge fund repo is often done at "zero or near-zero" haircuts [S153][S154a], which is why a proposal for minimum haircuts is a real constraint.

5.20 War and shocks: the two stress tests of 2026

@@f54@@
Figure 54. 2026 shock timeline. Sources as marked: Hedgeweek round-ups [S225][S223][S220], Bank of England [S240][S241], ECB [S247], Fed and BoE decisions [S244][S246], FinanceFeeds compilation [S238], data vendors [S249][S250]. The Situational Awareness figures are a secondary compilation with wide ranges.
Key term: crowding

Many funds holding the same positions. Harmless until a shock, when everyone tries to sell the same thing to the same buyers at once. The IMF says financial stress "has become more correlated with hedge fund losses since 2020" [S152]. Crowding is why platforms value information their rivals do not have, which is one reason in-house corporate access desks exist.

5.21 Performance: who won and who lost

@@f55@@
Figure 55. Who won and lost. Every bar is a press estimate; dates as labelled. Sources [S127][S145l][S161][S222][S220][S249].

Three readings of this chart, all defensible. First: 2025 was excellent for almost everyone and the industry's best year since 2009 [S150a]. Second: in 2026 the big platforms are doing what they promise, positive returns with a fraction of the market's swings, in a year when the market itself is the winner; "Most of the funds remain behind the US equity market this year" [S220]. Third: dispersion is enormous. Point72 at +14.5% and Balyasny at +0.5% are the same business model. Which teams you have, and how much crowded AI exposure they carried into July, decided the year.

5.22 The shake-out: the middle disappears

The model is not dying; the number of firms that can afford it is shrinking. Multi-manager AUM hit a record $428bn across 57 platforms, up 16% in 2025 after a pause in 2023 and 2024 [S158] Reported (Goldman Sachs data via secondary sources). At the same time Eisler wound down after -14.3% [S161]; Atlantic Wolf ($3bn), Taproot, Eminence ($8bn) and AB Arya closed in 2026 [S162]; liquidations jumped to 129 in the first quarter [S150d]. Even a record launch struggled: Jain Global raised $5.3bn in 2024, made about $1.8bn of gross trading profit but only 3.7% net in 2025, and in April 2026 agreed to return about $6bn of outside money and run Millennium's capital alone [S143][S229] Reported. The top two took opposite paths to the same capacity problem: Citadel returned about $5bn of 2025 profits and shrank to about $67bn [S165]; Millennium is raising a record ~$20bn while already at about $92bn [S221]. LCH Investments' Rick Sopher on the top firms: they "have periodically either closed to new subscriptions or returned capital, recognising that carefully controlling asset growth is a good basis for generating significant gains" [S134].

5.23 Technology and AI

Barclays finds 55% of investors have put AI into their investment process and 75% into non-investment workflows; discretionary managers are "embedding quantitative tools to expand coverage capacity without proportional headcount" [S171]. Quant multi-strategy is the most wanted strategy among allocators [S139b]. Systematic funds have handled shocks better: up 4% in March 2025 while stock-pickers lost 2.4% [S163]; trend-followers "outpaced discretionary global macro" in 2026 for the first time since 2022 [S162]. Millennium announced an AI lab in June and an Anthropic co-development of a "digital risk analyst" in August, with its CIO stressing "keeping human judgment at the center" [S99][S117]. The friction: 69% of large managers say broker data licensing blocks AI use [S209].

5.24 Geography: London and the Gulf

London is Europe's hedge fund capital and Millennium's largest office outside the US, with a co-head of global equities relocated there and a senior equities recruiter hired from Schonfeld in May 2026 [S231]. Two pressures work against it. First, tax: "a $20m buyout is tax-free in Dubai" against roughly $9m of UK tax, per an eFinancialCareers analysis, and one manager says "This is why the UK government is talking about imposing an exit tax" [S236] Reported, anonymous. Brevan Howard's Abu Dhabi office grew from 5 people in 2023 to 150 by late 2025 [S145m]; funds kept Gulf offices open through March's missile attacks [S235]. Second, the shrinking listed market: 23 London IPOs in 2025 and 7 in the first half of 2026, recovering from a near-dead 2024 but small, while CRH, Smurfit Westrock and Flutter all moved to New York-only listings in 2026 [S254][S255]. Fewer listed companies means fewer things for equity hedge funds to trade in London and scarcer meetings with their management.

@@c5D@@
Chapter 5D

How to talk about it

Three lengths of explanation, ten lines you can use, five traps, and the opinions worth forming.

@@f56@@
Figure 56. Three lengths of explanation. Figures as sourced in chapters 5A and 5C [S150a][S150c][S158][S157][S220][S225][S238][S240].

5.25 Ten lines you can use

  1. "The classic hedge fund takes less market risk than an index fund. Its risks are leverage and crowding, not the market."
  2. "Absolute return versus relative return is the real difference. Everything else follows from it."
  3. "Hedge funds are lightly regulated on what they may buy and heavily regulated on conduct, because their investors are professionals."
  4. "The industry is at a record $5.6tn, and almost all the new money is going to firms over $5bn."
  5. "Multi-manager platforms are about 8% of hedge fund assets but a far bigger share of market activity, because they run four to six times leverage."
  6. "Pass-through means investors pay the fund's actual costs. That is fine while net returns are good, which is why the fee fight is really an argument about performance."
  7. "2026 had two stress tests: the Iran shock in March and the AI reversal in July. Both were leverage-and-crowding events, and the big platforms mostly absorbed them."
  8. "Citadel gave money back and Millennium is raising a record amount. Two answers to the same capacity problem."
  9. "Regulators are not proposing to cap hedge fund leverage. They are squeezing it through the banks that lend to hedge funds, which favours the biggest funds."
  10. "Eisler is the cautionary tale: a $3 to 4bn platform whose losses came from costs, not trades."

5.26 Five traps

  • Quoting a private firm's numbers as fact. Say "press estimates" or "its own website says". Millennium's AUM moved from about $70bn to $92bn in under two years across different sources.
  • "Hedge funds beat the market." They do not aim to. In 2026 almost none did. Explain what they do aim for.
  • "MiFID II banned bundled research." It required separate payment; the UK and EU have since partly reversed that. If you raise regulation, get the dates right (Part 15 of the main guide).
  • Treating all hedge funds as one thing. Bridgewater (+34% in 2025) and Brevan Howard (+0.8%) are both macro funds. Name the type.
  • Using "edge" carelessly. Near a listed company, "edge" sounds like inside information. Say "differentiated view" or "better analysis".

5.27 Opinions worth forming

Your opinion goes here

Has the multi-manager model peaked? For: outflows in 2024, investors keeping 41c, closures. Against: record AUM, +16% growth, top firms oversubscribed. A defensible middle: "peaked for the mid-tier, not the top." Is the industry good for markets? For: liquidity, price discovery, absorbing Treasury issuance (Cayman funds bought 37% of net issuance since 2022 [S155b]). Against: crowded, leveraged unwinds amplify shocks, as the BoE found [S154b]. Should London worry? For: tax, listings, Gulf competition. Against: Millennium and others are building out London equities now. Pick sides, and say what evidence would move you.

@@p6@@
Part 6

The role's own industry: corporate access and research regulation

Why paying for access to company management became a regulated, priced, rationed service: bundled commissions, the FCA's 2014 ban, MiFID II unbundling in 2018, the 2024 to 2026 reversal that left corporate access out of scope, why in-house buy-side desks exist, who supplies access, and the current issues.

@@c6A@@
Chapter 6A

The corporate access and investment research industry from zero

How meetings with management used to be paid for, why regulators broke that model, why the UK and EU have partly rebuilt it, and why corporate access is the one thing they never re-bundled. This is the highest-leverage technical thread for this role.

@@f57@@
Figure 57. Three eras of paying for research and access. Every date is from the primary regulator document cited in Part 15 [S180][S181][S182][S184][S188][S199][S200].

6.1 Era 1: bundled commissions

For decades, a fund manager paid a broker a commission per trade, out of the client's money, and the broker "gave back" research, analyst calls and company meetings. In the US this is "soft dollars", protected by a 1975 safe harbour. In the UK it was "dealing commission". Nobody priced the meeting; it came free with the trading. The regulator's objection was simple: clients paid for services they never saw, and managers chose brokers for the perks rather than for execution quality Inferred framing.

The UK moved first. A 2012 regulator review found "the majority of investment managers had inadequate controls and oversight when acquiring research goods and services from brokers" and, specifically on corporate access: "None of the investment managers we visited could justify to us how Corporate Access met the evidential criteria for research under our rules to allow them to pay for it with dealing commissions" [S180] Confirmed. The industry's own numbers explain why the regulator cared: a Thomson Reuters Extel survey around 2012 reportedly found the share of commission allocated to corporate access had nearly doubled in three years to 27% (snippet only, not relied on), and the regulator estimated roughly £500m a year of UK commission was spent on access [S3] Reported.

The 2014 rule that created your job

FCA Policy Statement PS14/7, May 2014, effective 2 June 2014. It inserted a legal definition of a "corporate access service" into the rulebook, added corporate access to the list of things that may not be bought with dealing commission, and told managers who attend bundled events like conferences to "disaggregate the discrete element of substantive research" from the access and pay only for the research part with commission [S180] Confirmed. Paying for access stayed legal, from the firm's own money: a manager "may decide to pay this fee from their own resources". From this date, corporate access in the UK is a distinct, separately paid product. That is the origin of buy-side corporate access desks as budget-owning functions.

6.2 Era 2: MiFID II unbundling (3 January 2018)

MiFID II extended the logic across the EU and to all research. "Firms receiving research were required to either pay for research themselves from their own resources (P&L model) or agree a separate research charge with their clients (research payment account, or RPA model)" [S181] Confirmed. In the UK the rules live in COBS 2.3A (inducements) and COBS 2.3B (research payments).

On corporate access, ESMA's 2017 Q&A is the key text: "ESMA does not consider that arranging meetings is research"; corporate access "should be considered a discrete service"; a firm "can also treat corporate access as a commercial service and pay for it appropriately from its own resources"; and a firm wishing to meet a company "has the option to approach them directly and/or pay for a third party corporate access service provider" [S185][S13] Confirmed. That last sentence is the regulatory licence for in-house buy-side desks.

What unbundling did

  • Budgets collapsed. The FCA's 2019 review of 40 firms found research budgets down "20% to 30%", about £70m saved for investors in the first half of 2018 alone and "nearly £1 billion over 5 years" [S191] Confirmed. A CFA Institute survey found 54% of sell-side respondents saw fewer analysts and around half saw reduced small and mid-cap coverage [S192].
  • Brain drain. Substantive Research estimates the sell side lost "7,500 years of net experience" between 2018 and 2021 [S205] Reported.
  • Access went direct. The same FCA review recorded "a general increase in the proportion of corporate access meetings arranged directly between an issuer and asset manager without broker intermediation" [S191]. Once a broker meeting had a price, companies and investors cut out the middleman.
  • Small caps suffered. In a 2025 German and Austrian survey, 78% of smaller companies saw reduced sell-side coverage and 56% said investor access got harder [S187]. The UK's partial fix in 2022: research and corporate access on companies under £200m market cap became "acceptable minor non-monetary benefits", meaning brokers can provide them free without breaching inducement rules [S190][S15] Confirmed.
  • US friction. US brokers had relied on SEC no-action relief to accept cash for research without being treated as investment advisers. The SEC let it lapse on 3 July 2023 [S193][S196]. European managers now report a "competitive disadvantage" versus US peers, including "the ability to meet with the corporates they need to meet with" [S207].

6.3 Era 3: the reversal, exactly

Get these right. Precision here is the single most differentiating thing a candidate for this role can show.

DateDocumentWhat it didEffective
10 Jul 2023UK Investment Research Review (Rachel Kent) [S183]Seven recommendations, including "additional optionality" to pay for research by combining its cost with execution charges, under guardrails. Corporate access was not a headline recommendation; respondents asked for it to be reviewedn/a
Apr 2024FCA CP24/7 [S181]Consulted on "payment optionality". 44 responsesn/a
Jul 2024FCA PS24/9 [S181]New "joint payments" option in COBS 2.3B.25R to 33G: research and execution may be paid together again, subject to a written policy, a method for separately identifying the research cost, fair allocation across clients, an annual budget not linked to trading volumes, price benchmarking and value assessment, and client disclosure. Corporate access explicitly out of scope (see below). The sub-£200m corporate access exemption was retained1 Aug 2024
Nov 2024FCA CP24/21 [S182]Consulted on extending the option to pooled funds (UCITS and AIF managers). Confirmed the small-company corporate access exemption is unaffectedn/a
9 May 2025FCA PS25/4 [S188][S189]Extended joint payments to UCITS management companies and AIFMs; for retail funds adoption counts as a "significant change" requiring notice to investors9 May 2025, immediately
14 Nov 2024EU Listing Act: Regulation 2024/2809 and Directive 2024/2811 [S184][S198]Amended MiFID II to allow joint payments for research on issuers of any size (the 2021 rule had capped it at €1bn market cap), with conditions: inform clients, publish a policy, written agreement with a remuneration method, annual quality assessmentTranspose by 5 Jun 2026
8 Apr 2025ESMA technical advice [S184]Detailed rules for the new EU regimen/a
2 Jun 2026Commission Delegated Directive (EU) 2026/374 [S199]Removes the €1bn cap; research charges must not be linked to transaction volumes; strengthens annual assessment6 Jun 2026
15 Jul 2026European Commission infringement notices [S200]"18 Member States failed to communicate full transposition" of the Listing Act Directive, including France, Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland and Polandn/a
The sentence that matters most: corporate access was NOT re-bundled

FCA PS24/9, paragraph 3.53: "A sizeable portion of the respondents noted that the inducement rules around corporate access should be reviewed and consequently corporate access should be incorporated into the items that can be paid for with the new payment option or when utilising an RPA, as it would result in closer global alignment and enable smaller asset managers to get more corporate access." The FCA's answer: "These are all out of scope of this consultation" [S181] Confirmed, primary. No later FCA consultation revisiting this was found as of 4 September 2026. So in the UK a buy-side firm still has to pay for broker access above £200m from its own resources, go direct, or accept only what qualifies as a minor benefit. That is why the desk has its own budget logic, its own broker vote, and an origination channel.

Say this in the interview (only if the conversation goes there)

"The UK re-allowed bundled research payments from August 2024 and extended that to funds in May 2025, and the EU followed from June 2026. But corporate access was ruled out of scope in PS24/9. So access is still a separately valued service, which is exactly why a desk that tracks consumption and runs a broker vote exists." Keep it to two sentences and defer to them.

What the buy side actually did after PS24/9

Very little, so far. Substantive Research's surveys of the largest managers: in May 2024, 76.5% said they would not change their research process and 85% were paying from P&L [S203]; in December 2024, 80% of UK and European managers were still P&L-funded [S205]; in November 2025, 87% predicted at least half of budgets would be client-funded within two years [S207]; in April 2026, budgets had grown 1% in 2025, "driven entirely by US firms", with US budgets up 40 basis points of AUM since 2022 against 2 basis points in Europe, and adoption of the FCA option described as "slow" with a switch expected only in the second half of 2026 [S208][S256] Reported, consistent series. Hedge funds are typically P&L payers by nature; the joint-payment option matters more to long-only peers. But if long-only wallets re-open in late 2026, brokers may re-price access for everyone Inferred.

6.4 Why in-house buy-side corporate access teams exist

This is the strategic answer to "why does my job exist?" Four causes, all sourced:

  1. Regulation made broker access a priced, controlled service (2014 UK, 2018 EU) and explicitly allowed firms to "approach [issuers] directly" [S180][S185].
  2. Companies prefer direct contact. "Just under half of meetings between companies and investors are arranged via sell-side corporate access"; almost half of buy-siders are "much more likely" to take a meeting arranged directly versus 13% via a broker; 84% of IR officers rate direct access eight or more out of ten [S211][S212] Reported. Only "less than a quarter of buy-side respondents have a dedicated corporate access desk", so in-house desks are a large-firm phenomenon and being on one puts you at the front of the trend [S211].
  3. Scale. At a platform with over 300 teams, dozens of pods want the same CEO. A desk aggregates demand, allocates scarce slots and prevents duplicate asks. A multi-manager head reports "1,000+ headquarters meeting invitations annually" [S10].
  4. Data and compliance. A central desk holds the consumption data that drives the broker vote ("it's the firms that drive interactions (analyst meetings, corporate access engagements etc.) that now win increased market share" [S206]) and can evidence that access was not an unlawful inducement and that meetings were logged for market-abuse purposes (section 1.8).

Millennium's own structure fits: a Services desk for the broker channel and a sectorised Origination team for the direct channel [S42]. Long-only peers built earlier: Fidelity's team dates its Boston coverage to 2001 [S5]; hedge funds including Citadel, Balyasny, Millennium and Point72 were building by 2016 [S9].

6.5 Who supplies access: the competitive map

SupplierWhoWhat is known
Bank corporate access desksEvery bulge bracket and mid-cap broker: JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, Goldman, UBS, BofA, Jefferies, BarclaysJPMorgan ranked first by research payments among large managers in 2024, Jefferies second, Morgan Stanley third [S205]. Bulge-bracket pricing rose 1.5% in the first half of 2025 while specialists cut [S206]. Desks "may manage 200 to 300 clients" each [S29]
UK corporate brokersPeel Hunt, Deutsche Numis, Panmure Liberum, Cavendish (Cenkos and finnCap), CanaccordRetained by listed companies; run roadshow calendars and board feedback [S36][S37]. Consolidating: Deutsche bought Numis (2023), Panmure and Liberum merged (2024) [S213]. Peel Hunt's research and distribution revenue was £26.1m in its 2025 financial year, and it noted UK equity outflows in 46 of 47 months to April 2025 [S219] Confirmed
Expert networksGLG, AlphaSights, Third Bridge, Guidepoint, DialecticaAbout $3bn market in 2025, growing about 12% a year; GLG's share fell from 51% to 24% in a decade [S216] Reported. Only about 2% of research budgets [S204]. Adjacent to access, not access itself
IR advisory firmsFTI, Brunswick, Edelman Smithfield, ICR, EdisonAdvise companies on targeting investors; increasingly organise direct meetings [S12][S215]
Conference organisers and exchangesBank conferences dominate; exchanges organise someConferences carry "up to 80% of investor access" for many companies; participation up 51% since 2019 [S215] Reported, secondary
Technology platformsBloomberg, Dealogic (A2 Access), S&P Ipreo, WeConvene, ingage, OpenExchange, Q4, Irwin, FactSetUnified calendars, request workflows, notes into CRMs [S28][S31][S32][S33]. Millennium built its own portal instead

6.6 Current issues

Virtual versus in-person

Virtual fell to about 13% of corporate access activity by 2023 [S215]; 93% of German and Austrian issuers still see value in face-to-face, though 82% expect more digital formats [S187]. Investors worry that a return to in-person "will give them less opportunity to engage with senior management" [S214]. For the desk: logistics-heavy, conference-season work, with video for routine formats.

Shrinking public markets, especially London

London had 23 IPOs in 2025 raising £2.1bn, up from 18 raising £778m in 2024; the first half of 2026 saw 7 raising £577m [S255][S254] Confirmed. Delistings have exceeded new listings every year since 2022 (snippet only). CRH, Smurfit Westrock and Flutter all moved to New York-only listings in 2026 (company releases, snippets). Fewer issuers and fewer intermediaries make each management contact scarcer and more valuable.

Private markets

PISCES, the FCA's new private-share trading venue, approved the London Stock Exchange as first operator in August 2025 [S218]. Private companies are a new class of "issuer" for corporate access.

Small-cap access gap

The FCA retained the sub-£200m exemption because small caps struggle for access [S181]; the Kent Review's proposed research platform and the EU's issuer-sponsored research code are the policy responses [S183][S201]. This is where origination earns its keep.

ESG and governance demand

Issuers report governance content "rising in relevance" and expect access to become "more thematic, more targeted, and more self-directed" [S187]. The FCA confirmed in 2014 that stewardship research can be "substantive research" [S180].

AI in research workflows

77% of large managers now run firm-wide generative AI; broker research is the most-wanted machine-readable input; the main barrier is broker licensing (69%) [S209] Reported. For the desk: are meeting notes captured for internal tools, and how do MAR rules shape that?

What PMs value now

Meetings top the broker vote: 1x1 company meetings (82%), analyst visits (68%), conferences (58%) [S186]. Access to senior management is the scarce good. Access, not reports, wins wallet share [S206].

Your opinion goes here

Should corporate access be brought inside the joint-payment regime, as "a sizeable portion" of respondents asked? Case for: global alignment, and smaller managers could afford more access. Case against: bundling access with commission recreates the 2012 problem, where clients paid for meetings they never saw and brokers rationed slots to the biggest commission payers. Decide. The author leans against, because the buy-side desk's whole value rests on access being priced and tracked explicitly.

7.2 The twelve stories that matter, ranked

Each card: what happened, why it matters to Millennium, why it matters to corporate access specifically, and one question or opinion you could raise.

1. Millennium in talks to raise a record ~$20bn

Reuters, 29 Jul 2026; Hedgeweek citing Bloomberg, 30 Jul 2026 [S221][S226] Confirmed (press)

What. Millennium, already managing "more than $92 billion" with "more than 6,800" employees and "more than 340 teams", is raising about $20bn in two tranches of "callable" capital (commitments drawn over time), led by president Ajay Nagpal. Part will replace outside investors in partner firms such as Jain Global. In 2024 it took $10bn of $20bn offered.

Millennium. Closer to a $100bn firm. More pods, more PMs, more London hiring, and more pressure to keep returns steady at size.

Corporate access. More fundamental equity teams means more meeting demand. The desk must scale: broker relationships, direct sourcing, systems.

Ask. "With capital arriving as callable commitments, how does the desk plan capacity for new pods that arrive in waves?"

2. Millennium flat in August, up 8.2% year to date, against an S&P 500 up about 19%

Hedgeweek citing Business Insider, 4 Sep 2026; Hedgeweek citing Bloomberg, 4 Aug 2026 [S220][S223][S222] Reported

What. Up 10.5% in the first half, down 2.1% in July as the AI trade reversed, flat in August. Peers to end-August: Citadel +12.1%, ExodusPoint +4.9%, Balyasny +0.5%. Point72 led the first half at +14.5%. "Most of the funds remain behind the US equity market this year."

Millennium. A respectable low-volatility year, not a market-beating one. Allocators paying pass-through costs will raise the cash-hurdle debate. Do not describe 2026 as a great year.

Corporate access. When crowded AI longs hurt, differentiated insight from management contact is the antidote to crowding.

Opinion. "About 8% with a fraction of the market's volatility is what the product is supposed to look like. The question allocators will ask is whether that beats cash plus fees."

3. Jain Global returns outside money to run Millennium capital only

Hedgeweek citing Bloomberg, 27 Apr and 2 Sep 2026 [S228][S229] Reported

What. Bobby Jain, Millennium's former co-CIO, launched with $5.3bn in July 2024, made about $1.8bn gross but net returns were thin (3.7% in 2025). He will now manage over $5bn for Millennium alone, keeping his firm operationally independent.

Millennium. A template for absorbing talent without an acquisition. Even a $5bn launch by a star could not match platform economics.

Corporate access. A real operational question: do partner firms sit inside Millennium's corporate access perimeter, and how are information barriers handled?

4. First-ever stake sale: 15% for about $2bn, valuing the firm at about $14bn

Hedgeweek citing Bloomberg, 4 Nov 2025 [S227] Reported, widely covered

What. Englander sold equity for the first time in 36 years, to institutions, wealthy clients via bank wealth platforms, and Millennium executives, arranged by Goldman's Petershill. Millennium said it "reinforces the durability of the firm, supports the longevity of our business". The earlier reported BlackRock talks (December 2024) did not result in a BlackRock stake; see chapter 2A.

Millennium. Succession and institutionalisation. Outside owners care about durable infrastructure, not one person's contacts.

Corporate access. Platform services become part of the valuation story and get measured.

5. Bank of England: hedge fund equity leverage at a record; gilt repo borrowing fell 40% after the Iran shock

BoE Financial Stability Report and Governor's remarks, 7 Jul 2026 [S240][S241] Confirmed, primary

What. "There has been a significant rise in hedge fund leverage in equity markets, creating risks, including via the prime brokers." Equity prime-brokerage balances up about 40% in a year, concentrated in semiconductors. Hedge funds cut gilt repo borrowing about 40% in the five weeks after the conflict began, amplifying yield moves. A second system-wide stress exercise is under way with asset managers.

Millennium. A large user of leverage and gilt repo. UK scrutiny of multi-manager leverage is rising.

Corporate access. Indirect: a well-run, well-documented platform is a regulatory asset.

6. Situational Awareness collapses; Citadel buys the book

FinanceFeeds compiling CNBC, FT and Bloomberg, 31 Jul 2026 [S238] Reported, secondary compilation; ranges wide

What. A two-year-old AI-thematic fund reportedly grew to $20 to 45bn on about four times leverage, lost 27 to 54% on core holdings in July, hit margin calls and sold its entire public book to Citadel on 30 July.

Millennium. The unwind drove July losses in AI-exposed pods. Citadel's opportunism widened the year-to-date gap.

Corporate access. Crowding in AI names is the argument for proprietary, non-consensus insight from management contact rather than the same sell-side calendar as everyone else.

Ask. "After July, did demand shift toward second-tier AI supply-chain companies, or away from the theme?"

7. The talent war goes to court

Hedgeweek citing Bloomberg, 20 and 23 Apr, 28 Aug 2026 [S232][S233][S234] Reported; allegations only

What. Schonfeld sued a PM it says agreed to join and reversed to stay at Millennium ($11m claimed). Millennium is seeking about $2.5m from a Hong Kong PM who accepted then abandoned an offer. "Interception trades" target PMs during gardening leave; star packages "exceeding $100 million".

Millennium. On both sides. Talent cost is the core expense passed through to investors.

Corporate access. Fast, high-quality onboarding, including access to management meetings from week one, is part of what makes a PM show up and stay. The Tokyo posting lists onboarding new investment professionals as a desk duty [S43].

8. Millennium builds London equities

eFinancialCareers, 12 May 2026; Hedgeweek, 14 Mar 2025 [S231][S62] Reported

What. Schonfeld's former head of EMEA fundamental equity business development joined to find equity PMs in London; a Goldman London co-head of equities hired in February 2026; co-global head of equities Peter Santoro relocated to London in late 2025; further senior PM hires from Maven and Eisler.

Corporate access. This is your internal client base growing. More European fundamental PMs means more UK and European company meetings, more conference coverage, more roadshow requests. Directly relevant to "primarily across EMEA".

Ask. "Given the European equities build-out, how is the London desk's coverage split between UK, Continental Europe and emerging markets?"

9. Research budgets: US up 40bp since 2022, Europe up 2bp; UK payment optionality adoption "slow"

Substantive Research, 27 Apr 2026; FCA PS25/4 [S256][S257] Reported (survey) / Confirmed (rule)

What. 73% of European managers say they are at a disadvantage to US peers, including in "accessing... the corporate access they need". Few UK firms have switched to joint payments; a switch is expected in the second half of 2026. EU joint payments apply from 6 June 2026, but 18 member states missed the transposition deadline [S200].

Corporate access. Directly on point. If long-only wallets re-open, brokers may re-price access. Corporate access itself remains outside the UK joint-payment option (chapter 6A).

Ask. "Has the London entity looked at the joint-payment option, and does corporate access sit inside or outside that budget?"

10. Central-bank week is the week after your interview

BoE 30 Jul; Fed 29 Jul; ONS via GLA, Aug 2026 [S246][S244][S245][S253] Confirmed

What. UK CPI prints 16 September, the MPC decides 17 September with three members already voting to hike, and the FOMC meets 15 to 16 September. Gilts above 5% reflect energy-driven inflation and fiscal worries after July's change of Prime Minister and Chancellor. The Fed minutes warn that a downgrade of AI expectations "might lead to a broad-based repricing of assets".

Corporate access. Financing costs, consumer demand and AI capex are the questions PMs want answered by management this month.

Ask. "What do PMs want from UK consumer-facing management teams in a week like this?"

11. London listings recover from a very low base; big names leave for New York

EY IPO Eye, 8 Jul and 6 Jan 2026 [S254][S255] Confirmed

What. Seven London IPOs in the first half of 2026 raising £577m, helped by listing reforms and a three-year stamp duty holiday for new listings; only two in Q1 because of the war. CRH, Smurfit Westrock and Flutter all cancelled London lines in 2026 (company releases, snippets). EY: "For UK issuers, the focus is shifting from 'if' to 'when'."

Corporate access. A shrinking listed universe raises the value of each management contact, and pre-IPO "early-look" meetings are a growing workflow with their own compliance walls.

12. Dubai stays open through the Iran war; the UAE keeps pulling London talent

Hedgeweek citing Bloomberg, 26 Mar 2026; eFinancialCareers, 20 Feb 2026 [S235][S236] Reported

What. After missile attacks, Millennium told staff it was "exploring relocation options for employees who prefer to work elsewhere but intends to maintain its office in the city". Zero income tax keeps drawing PMs from London; one manager: "This is why the UK government is talking about imposing an exit tax."

Corporate access. Gulf-listed companies and sovereign investors are a growing meeting market that London's time zone can cover.

Source uncertain: what could not be verified

Millennium's monthly returns for March to May 2026 from a credible outlet (one editorial site claimed about $1.5bn of losses in early March, unsourced, not relied on). Any FCA data on take-up of joint payments. Any 2026 FCA statement on corporate access specifically. The Autumn Budget date. Non-dom departure data. Any 2026 news on Millennium's London office. Several Bloomberg originals were paywalled and are listed in the Reading List with headlines only.

7.3 Sources to follow from now on

  • Hedgeweek: free, fast rewrites of Bloomberg, FT and Business Insider hedge fund scoops. Search "Millennium" around the 3rd to 5th of each month for prior-month returns.
  • Business Insider (Bradley Saacks, Alex Morrell), often free via Yahoo Finance: monthly multi-strategy scorecards and pod-shop internals.
  • Bloomberg (Nishant Kumar in London, Hema Parmar in New York): primary scoops; paywalled, use Hedgeweek summaries.
  • Reuters hedge fund desk (Nell Mackenzie, Carolina Mandl): free, citable.
  • FT (Costas Mourselas, Harriet Agnew): multi-manager fees, the London hub; paywalled.
  • eFinancialCareers (Sarah Butcher): London people moves, pay, UAE flows.
  • Substantive Research (Mike Carrodus): research budget and corporate access pricing surveys.
  • IR Magazine / IR Impact: corporate access surveys from the company side.
  • Bank of England Financial Stability Report (July, December) and MPC minutes; FCA policy statements and Market Watch; ESMA Listing Act pages; IMF GFSR (April, October).
  • EY IPO Eye quarterly for London listings; Trading Economics for quick rate and index levels with dates.

Chapter 7B

What has changed since 5 September

A senior interviewer will assume you have kept up. This part is the update from a fresh sweep on 17 September of Millennium, the platform sector and the regulation that governs the desk.

7.4 The three items to have ready

1. Millennium nears $100bn; $22bn closes on 1 October

Bloomberg, 7 September, read in full via syndication [S400]; Hedgeweek 8 September [S401] Confirmed as press reporting. Assets about $97bn, more than double six years ago. On 1 October the firm closes $22bn of new commitments, calling $2bn that day and the rest over four years, with a roughly $3bn less-liquid credit raise under discussion. New money faces a five-year withdrawal restriction, longer than peers' three to four. Wealthy individuals are reported at 30 to 40% of assets. Jain Global ($5bn) and Albar ($1.5bn) are now exclusive to Millennium.
For the desk: more capital means more seats and more external teams to serve. Say: "The $22bn closing on 1 October is the clearest sign the client base of a central desk keeps growing."

2. August: flat; +8.2% for the year

Hedgeweek, 4 September [S402] Reported. Millennium flat in August after July's -2.1% AI-stock unwind; Citadel +0.1% (+12.1% YTD); Balyasny -0.7% (+0.5%); ExodusPoint +1.4% (+4.9%); S&P 500 +2.6% and about +12% YTD.
For the desk: a year in which the firm trails the index is exactly when consistency, not the headline number, is the pitch. Say: "Flat August, eight per cent for the year, against a market up twelve: the product is the drawdown profile, not the return."

3. Regulation: nothing new on access; two enforcement signals

No FCA or ESMA change to payment optionality, inducements or corporate access rules in the window [S415]. Two items a senior interviewer may raise: the Upper Tribunal upheld the FCA's ban on Crispin Odey on 10 September, fine set at £1,529,374 [S413] Confirmed, primary; and the FCA's Primary Market Bulletin 65 (28 August) reviewed delayed disclosure of inside information under UK MAR [S415].
For the desk: conduct and inside-information handling are live enforcement themes. Say: "The rules for paying for access haven't moved since 2024; what has moved is enforcement on conduct and on how issuers handle inside information, which is the perimeter the desk works inside."

Part 8

Forming your own view

A method for holding a view you can defend: claim, evidence, limit. Six questions argued both ways, and how to build "why Millennium" from raw material rather than a script.

@@c8A@@
Chapter 8A

chapter 8A

Forming your own view

The candidate wants to defend opinions, not recite facts. This part lays out the arguments on both sides of the six questions most likely to come up, and a method for building a view you can hold under pressure.

8.1 The method: claim, evidence, limit

A defensible opinion in a 30-minute interview has three parts and takes 30 seconds. Claim: one sentence. Evidence: one or two sourced facts, with dates. Limit: the one thing that would change your mind. Interviewers push on the limit; if you name it first, the push becomes a conversation instead of a correction. Never claim more precision than the source has. "Press estimates put it at" beats a number stated as fact.

1. Claim"The pod model has peaked for mid-tier platforms, not for the top four."
2. EvidenceEisler closed after -14.3% driven by pass-through costs (Jan 2026); $39bn of $44.5bn Q1 2026 inflows went to $5bn+ firms.
3. Limit"If Millennium's 2026 ends below cash after fees, allocators' hurdle demands could bite even at the top."

8.2 Six questions, both sides

Q1. Is the multi-manager model past its peak?

Yes

  • Multi-strategy funds had net outflows of over $30bn in the year to June 2024, the first since 2016 [S159]
  • Investors kept roughly 41 to 59 cents per gross dollar [S157]; Balyasny went 15.2% gross to 2.8% net in 2023 [S156]
  • Eisler, Atlantic Wolf, Taproot, Eminence, AB Arya closed 2025 to 2026 [S161][S162]
  • Nine-figure PM packages and lawsuits over "gazumping" [S160b][S232]

No

  • Record $5.6tn industry capital; inflows concentrated in $5bn+ firms [S150c][S150b]
  • Multi-manager AUM at a record $428bn, +16% in 2025 [S158]
  • Millennium raising $10bn-plus again in 2026; Jain Global and Albar chose to become Millennium pods [S107][S102][S110]
  • 21.6% of allocation intentions target multi-strategy [S162]
Author's view, for you to accept or reject

Peaked for the middle, not the top. The number of platforms that can afford the model has shrunk; the top four or five are consolidating the talent and the capital. Limit: a year in which the top platforms return less than cash after fees.

Q2. Is pass-through fair?

Fair

  • Investors bought a 14% annualised return with one down year [S111][S115]; beta about 0.24 to equities [S172]
  • "Everyone brings up the fees, but all I care about are net returns" [S160a]
  • Capacity is scarce; waiting lists exist [S111]

Unfair

  • Investors bear netting risk: winning pods are paid while losers are not refunded [S175][S104]
  • Pass-through funds the talent war: $11bn of Citadel's $12.5bn pass-through was compensation [S156]
  • Sixty-plus asset owners demand cash hurdles; most of Texas Teachers' managers agreed [S167a][S157]
Author's view

Fair while net returns beat what allocators can get elsewhere for the same volatility, and only then. Which means every cost centre, corporate access included, has to show its keep. Limit: a multi-year stretch below cash plus a margin.

Q3. Should corporate access be brought inside the joint-payment regime?

Yes

  • "A sizeable portion" of PS24/9 respondents asked for it: global alignment, and smaller managers could get more access [S181]
  • 73% of European managers say they are disadvantaged versus US peers on research and access [S207]
  • Separate payment constructs add operational complexity [S181]

No

  • The 2012 review found no manager could justify paying for access with commission [S180]; bundling recreates the problem
  • Brokers ration slots to the biggest commission payers; explicit pricing is what lets a buy-side desk track and allocate [S30][S39]
  • Companies prefer direct contact anyway [S212]
Author's view

No. The buy-side desk's value depends on access being priced and tracked explicitly. Limit: evidence that UK managers are losing meetings to US peers because of the rule, rather than because of budget choices.

Q4. Will origination replace the broker channel?

Yes, mostly

  • Half of buy-siders are "much more likely" to take a direct meeting versus 13% via a broker [S212]
  • The FCA itself recorded the shift to direct arrangement in 2019 [S191]
  • Brokers have withdrawn from small and mid caps [S187]

No

  • Conferences carry up to 80% of access for many companies, and participation is up 51% since 2019 [S215]
  • UK plcs' house brokers run the roadshow calendar [S36][S37]
  • A multi-manager head: "Our job isn't to replace brokers. It's to optimize how we consume corporate access" [S10]
Author's view

No replacement; a rebalancing. Brokers keep conferences and large-cap volume; origination wins the bespoke, mid-cap and hard-to-reach meetings. The desk's skill is knowing which channel to use for which request. Limit: a collapse in bank conference economics.

Q5. Does more meeting volume mean better investing?

Yes

  • Investors trade "heavily and profitably" around roadshows [S38]
  • Meetings top the broker vote at 82% [S186]
  • Hedge funds need "shorter feedback loops" [S11]

No

  • "Corporate access scaled on the assumption that more meetings equaled better engagement" [S11]
  • "It's not about taking a meeting for the sake of taking a meeting" [S8]
  • Every meeting is a pass-through cost and a compliance event
Author's view

Quality over count, which is exactly why the JD says "quantity and quality" and why consumption reports exist. Limit: a pod strategy where breadth of coverage genuinely is the edge.

Q6. Is hedge fund leverage a systemic problem regulators will constrain?

Yes

  • Top ten funds hold over a third of all hedge fund gross notional [S152]
  • BoE: equity prime-brokerage balances up about 40% in a year; hedge fund deleveraging amplified gilt moves in 2026 [S240][S241]
  • Fed: $830bn basis trade, top 50 funds about 90% [S155a]

Not directly

  • FSB: entity-level leverage limits are impractical for multi-strategy funds [S153]
  • Constraint arrives through prime-broker balance sheet and haircuts, not fund caps [S154d][S154c]
  • Multi-strategy funds' low beta is why allocators want them [S172]
Author's view

The constraint is coming, via banks' balance sheets and minimum repo margins rather than a leverage cap. The largest platforms with the deepest prime-broker relationships are best placed, which is another reason capital concentrates. Limit: a direct leverage rule for multi-strategy funds, which the FSB says is hard.

8.3 Building your "why Millennium" from raw material, not a script

An interviewer can tell a script from a view in one follow-up question. Build the answer from three layers and one personal fact.

  1. The firm, in your words. Pick one thing you find genuinely interesting about the model, not the biggest. Candidates: the netting problem (why risk is so tight); the allocator strategy (Jain Global coming home); the capital-terms bet (five-year liquidity while Citadel returns money); the "we never want to be the market" philosophy.
  2. The seat, in your words. Why this function is a real problem worth solving here: hundreds of independent pods, two channels, a portal, a broker vote, and a regulator that kept access outside the re-bundling rules. This is the hardest version of the corporate access problem in the industry.
  3. London, in your words. The EMEA hub, the equities build-out, and a rulebook that is changing in London specifically.
  4. The personal fact. Something you have actually done that maps to internal client service, allocation under scarcity, or data that someone relied on. Without this the other three layers are research, not motivation.
Don't say this

"Millennium is the best hedge fund in the world." It is not the best by returns (17th of 20 on Bloomberg's 2025 table) and both interviewers know it. "Largest, most diversified, most consistent" is defensible. "Best" is not.

The interview: process, Round 1 record, Round 2 plan and the question bank

The process as Millennium describes it, the Round 1 brief kept as a record of what was prepared, the 52-question bank with scaffolds, what Round 1 revealed, and the full question set for the two one-hour Round 2 interviews with Joe and with Chris, the Head of the Desk.

Chapter 9A

The interview

What Round 1 almost certainly is, what follows, a 52-question bank with scaffolds rather than scripts, and ten questions only a well-researched candidate could ask. The full bank is also in Question_Bank.md for rehearsal.

Status note

This chapter was written before Round 1, which took place on Monday 7 September 2026 with Katherine Hayes and Oliver Harvey and was passed. It is kept because the process description, the question bank and the scaffolds still apply to Round 2. Where it says "Monday" it means that Round 1 date. The Round 2 material starts in the next chapter.

9.1 The process

@@f58@@
Figure 58. The funnel. Steps 1 to 3 from the candidate's invitation and Millennium's student page [S261]; step 4 inferred from candidate reports for other non-investing seats [S262][S263]; see 9.2. As of 4 Sep 2026.

Millennium's own student page describes three steps: Screening ("Candidates are reviewed for eligibility"), Assessments ("to match with hiring teams"), and Interviews ("Technical and behavioral interviews") [S261] Confirmed. It says no financial markets experience is required, that it assesses "areas of interest, applicable skillsets, and potential", and that its interview advice is to review the posting and the website and "draw upon prior experiences, projects, and coursework" [S261]. Its stated goal is "to hire our analyst class from our internship program" [S261]. Scale: 190 interns globally in 2025 from about 50,000 applications; London was the largest hub outside the US with 57 of 239 open roles in January 2025 [S271][S271b] Reported. Programme length is not on the website; third parties say about ten weeks, June to August [S269][S270]. Ask.

The assessment you sat. Three independent 2026 prep sites say Millennium uses the Criteria Corp platform and, for most roles, the CCAT: 50 questions in 15 minutes, sometimes with a work-preference questionnaire [S265][S266][S267] Reported, unverified for this role. If that matches what you sat, it has done its job and will not be discussed. If you completed a work-preference questionnaire, be consistent with it on Monday.

9.2 What Round 1 is, with confidence levels

QuestionBest answerConfidence
How many rounds?Anecdotes for other Millennium non-investing intern seats cluster at two to three conversations after the assessment: a 30-minute video round, then one further round, sometimes two back-to-back 30-minute sessions or a senior "fit" chat [S262][S263]. The label "Round 1" confirms at least one more. Superdays of three to five interviews are reported only for quant and tech seats [S269]Medium
What is in the 30 minutes?Two desk-level interviewers (chapter 10A). Realistic split: 2 to 3 minutes introductions; 5 minutes CV, why us, why this role; 12 to 15 minutes of three to five behavioural or role-understanding questions; 5 minutes for your questions; bufferInferred
Technical?No test, case or market quiz is reported for business-services seats. "Technical" here means: can you explain what corporate access is, why a PM wants a meeting, how you would run a request list in Excel, and why compliance cares. Operations interviewees report a question on "global market conditions" [S263], so have one live view readyMedium-high
What follows?Most likely a second video round with the EMEA corporate access head or a senior Execution Services manager, more probing on judgement and fit; possibly an HR touchpoint. Offers are rolling, days to about three weeks [S265][S269]Low-medium
The one story to have ready

The only Millennium executive interview on interviewing that could be read says the favourite question is "Tell me about your favorite project", looking for self-initiated work that fixed something "nobody would ever touch because they were all afraid of breaking it", and flags 30-second answers and AI-written CVs as red flags [S277]. It was about technology hiring but the JD's "increase efficiencies" line says the same thing. Have one story where you improved a process nobody owned, with a number in it.

9.3 The question bank

Notation: T what is tested; S structure; F facts to weave in; X traps. Behavioural answers use STAR-R (Situation, Task, Action, Result, Reflection) in 60 to 90 seconds. Fill every scaffold with your own experience; a scripted answer collapses at the first follow-up.

A. Motivation

1. Tell me about yourself.
T Concision. S 60 seconds: degree and year; two experiences showing organisation, communication or data; why this seat now. F You fit the Dec 2027 to Jun 2028 window; humanities and social sciences are "a plus" [S260]. X Life story; over 90 seconds.
2. Why Millennium?
T Depth beyond the homepage. S Three specific reasons plus one personal one (section 9.3). F Hundreds of independent teams make access a service business with internal clients [S42]; two channels, three desks, a portal, a semi-annual vote [S40][S43]; stated intent to hire the analyst class from interns; London the largest non-US hub [S261][S271b]. X AUM with false precision; "prestige"; "best hedge fund".
3. Why corporate access, not an investing seat?
T Is this a fallback. S What you like about the work itself: organising scarce access, broker relationships, data and reporting, close to the investment process without being the stock-picker. F The desk exists because UK rules since 2014 require access to be sourced and paid for deliberately [S180]. X Any hint you plan to move to investing.
4. Why a hedge fund rather than a bank or long-only manager?
T Buy side versus sell side. S Sell side sells access as a product; buy side procures and allocates it for internal clients; at a multi-manager the allocation problem is hardest. X Disparaging banks; one interviewer appears to have started on a bank's corporate access desk.
5. What do you want from the internship?
T Realism. S Three things from the JD to learn (portal, allocation, consumption reporting) and one thing you bring. X "Exposure to PMs" as the main draw.
6. How did you hear about the role, and what else have you applied for?
T Honesty. F Two-application cap [S261]. X Claiming this is your only application if it is not.
7. What does our team do day to day?
T Preparation. S Paraphrase the JD's day-to-day line, then the two channels. X Describing sell-side logistics as the buy-side job.
8. Where do you see yourself in five years?
T Conversion fit. S Full-time on the platform side, owning broker relationships or the reporting and portal side; open. X "Portfolio manager."

B. Commercial awareness

9. What is happening in markets that matters to our PMs' meeting requests?
T Are you awake. S One EMEA theme for 45 seconds, linked to meeting demand. F chapter 7A: central-bank week after your interview; AI-trade reversal in July; London listings recovering. X Bluffing numbers. Say "as of this week".
10. What is a multi-manager fund, in your own words?
S Many independent teams under central limits and shared services; costs passed through; return is the average of uncorrelated bets. X Reciting limits you cannot source.
11. Why do buy-side firms have their own corporate access teams now?
F 2014 UK rule; 2018 MiFID II "discrete service"; companies prefer direct (half "much more likely" versus 13%) [S180][S185][S212]; brokers left small caps [S187]. X "MiFID II banned corporate access." It changed how it is paid for.
12. What do brokers get out of giving us meetings?
S Trading flow and goodwill; our consumption data feeds their vote [S39][S43]. X Implying per-slot purchase.
13. What could reduce the value of corporate access?
S Virtual lowering scarcity; direct platforms; AI commoditising note capture; tighter inducement rules; fewer listed companies. X Only "AI".
14. Who are Millennium's peers, and how do they run corporate access?
F section 4.1: Point72 dedicated team with Compliance; Balyasny one head with the commission wallet; Schonfeld under broker relations. X Peer AUM you cannot source.
15. Why is London important to Millennium?
F Largest non-US hub; whole-building Mayfair HQ; co-head of equities relocated; 2026 equities recruiter hire [S271b][S148][S231]. X Asserting an address; sources show two.

C. Behavioural

16. Prioritising several urgent requests at once.
T "Prioritization and urgency". S State the rule you used and whom you told. X "I did everything."
17. A mistake in detail-heavy work.
S The error, how you found it, whom you told, the check you built. X A trivial one; blaming a system.
18. A demanding senior stakeholder you could not satisfy.
S Clarify the real need; nearest deliverable; early expectations; escalate. X Pretending you always said yes.
19. Acting with incomplete information.
S Reversible step first; flag the assumption; confirm later. X "I waited."
20. Improving a process nobody asked you to.
T "Increase efficiencies"; the executive's favourite question [S277]. S What was broken, what changed, the saving. X No number.
21. A teammate not pulling their weight.
S Direct and kind; redistribute; protect the deliverable. X Blame.
22. Communicating something complicated in writing.
S Audience; answer first; result. The desk lives on email.
23. Pushing back on someone senior.
S Reason, alternative, outcome. X Stubbornness.
24. Handling repetitive admin.
S It is the foundation of trust; error-free; look for automation. X Sighing.
25. Running an event or logistics for many people.
T "Booking and confirming rooms and attendees". S Numbers, what went wrong, recovery.
26. A dataset others relied on.
S Source, checks, output, who used it. X A class exercise with no user.
27. Feedback that stung.
S Specific feedback, specific change. X Fake weaknesses.

D. Role understanding

28. What is corporate access?
F FCA definition [S2]; formats; two channels. X Calling it investor relations.
29. What does a PM want from a management meeting?
S Answers the filings do not give; tone and consistency; whether the thesis is tracking; competitive colour. Never inside information. X "An edge."
30. How would you allocate contested conference slots?
S Ranked requests with reasons; a rule (relevance, recency, group format); publish it; escalate ties; log the outcome. F Banks allocate by "investor tier, AUM, and fund mandate fit" [S275]; booking opens 4 to 6 weeks out [S30]. X First come first served alone.
31. Two PMs want the same CFO slot.
S Ask the broker for a second slot or group format; check need; loop in the head; never promise both. X Loudest wins.
32. What is MNPI and why does the desk care?
F Definition; UK MAR; the FCA says analysts are "not the public" and private issuer calls are "dissemination" [S21][S22]; the desk logs and routes meetings. X "Interns would never encounter this."
33. An executive says something that sounds material and non-public.
S Stop; report to Compliance; do not trade or share; know the path, do not filter. F Einhorn: declining to be wall-crossed was no defence [S19].
34. What is a consumption report for?
F Coverage gaps, broker value (feeds the semi-annual vote), conference planning [S260][S43].
35. What is a broker vote?
F Periodic scoring of brokers' services; 1x1 meetings top the list at 82% [S186]; Millennium's is semi-annual [S43]. X Over-claiming Millennium's method.
36. Broker-sourced versus originated: why both?
F Volume and conferences versus control, reach and independence; sectorised Origination team [S42][S47]. X "Originated is free."
37. What goes in a weekly forward-calendar email?
S Conferences by date and sector, request deadlines, NDRs in London, new this week, contacts. X No deadlines.
38. What is an NDR?
F Management tours investors without raising capital; about 65% broker-sponsored in a large US sample [S38]. X Confusing with an IPO roadshow.
39. How would you measure whether the team is doing a good job?
F "Access quality, utilization, costs, and team feedback" [S25]; hit rate; time to confirm; error rate. X Volume only.

E. Excel and data

40. How comfortable are you in Excel?
S Honest level; functions used for real (XLOOKUP, pivots, COUNTIFS, remove duplicates, validation); one maintained dataset. X Claiming VBA you cannot show later.
41. 400 requests, 12 teams, 60 slots: structure the spreadsheet.
S One row per request; team, requester, company, priority 1 to 3, rationale, last met, acceptable format; pivot by company; apply the rule; clean file for the broker, log for consumption. X Formulas before structure.
42. Checking a dataset before it goes to a PM.
S Totals reconcile; duplicates; blanks; date formats; broker spellings; second pair of eyes. X "I'd be careful."
43. Presenting data in PowerPoint.
S One chart, one message, one page.
44. CRMs or event tools?
S Any database or society tool; the hygiene you practised. X Pretending to know Ipreo or Dealogic.

F. Logistics

45 to 48. Dates and office attendance; right to work; other Millennium applications; anything on the CV to explain.
S Plain, factual. Programme length is not on the website; ask.

G. Curveballs

49. A broker cuts our conference requests by half. Next hour?
S Facts first; re-rank with the teams; ask for group alternatives; tell affected teams early with options. X Hiding it.
50. Two analysts from different teams in the same 1x1: a problem?
S Teams are independent; whether they may share is a house rule and a broker rule; check rather than assume.
51. Sell me on an hour in a meeting versus reading the transcript.
S Follow-ups, unscripted answers, tone, the relationship for next time. Thirty seconds.
52. What did you expect us to ask that we have not?
S Offer one from section D and answer it in 30 seconds.

9.4 Ten questions to ask them

  1. "The posting describes both sell-side broker-sourced and Millennium-originated access. Roughly what share of EMEA meetings comes through each channel today, and is the intern more involved in one?"
  2. "How do the consumption reports feed the strategy sessions: broker evaluation, conference planning, or both?"
  3. "When several teams request the same 1x1 at a conference, is there a written allocation rule or is it case by case?"
  4. "How does the London desk work with the Sector Specialist Origination team and Broker Relations day to day?"
  5. "The UK's payment optionality rules from 2024 cover research but corporate access was ruled out of scope. Has that changed how the desk values broker access, or how brokers behave towards you?"
  6. "What does the proprietary portal do that off-the-shelf platforms do not, and is there scope for an intern to improve it?"
  7. "For Business Services seats, what does a strong intern look like by week ten?"
  8. "Is there desk-specific training on the compliance side of management meetings, for example MNPI and restricted lists?"
  9. "Is EMEA meeting demand growing faster than broker supply, given the London equities build-out, and how does the desk cope?"
  10. "What are the next steps and the expected timeline after this round?"

Pick two or three. Questions 1 to 6 suit practitioners; 7 to 10 suit any panel. Process questions can also go to the coordinator by email.

9.5 Before Monday

  • Test Webex the day before; the browser version works if the app fails. Camera at eye level. One page of notes off-camera.
  • Rehearse aloud: questions 2, 3, 16, 20, 30, 32 and your one process-improvement story. Sixty to ninety seconds each.
  • Read Part 0's emergency version on Monday morning, then the Cheat Sheet.
  • Check Hedgeweek on Monday morning for any weekend Millennium news.
  • Have two questions from 8.4 written down. Say the interviewers' names on hand-over.
  • If audio drops, say so calmly. Composure under a glitch is itself a signal for a logistics seat.

9.6 The email, decoded

  • "The team would like to progress you." The decision was the desk's, not HR's. Katherine and Oliver wrote notes; those notes go to whoever interviews you next. Round 2 starts from what they said about you, so the debrief in chapter 9C matters.
  • "Campus Recruiter for the Corporate Access Intern position." Jessica Cresswell now owns scheduling. Reply to her promptly, warmly and briefly. She is also the person who will hear about any competing offers, and she will use that to set the pace.
  • "REQ-30221." Your Round 1 posting was REQ-30183. The public campus site still lists only REQ-30183 for London as of 17 September [S40][S51]. REQ-30221 is most likely the internal requisition for the hire rather than a different role; do not read anything into it, and do not mention it.
  • "Early next week to schedule." Expect the interview itself in the week of 21 September or the week after. Prepare as if it is Monday 21st.
  • "Other interview processes or competing offers." A normal question with a right answer. chapter 9E.
